attributes.body:
In our first らしい lesson, we discussed the auxiliary verb use of らしい. In this lesson we will focus on the 形容詞（けいようし）の一部（いちぶ） (auxiliary adjective) usage. An auxiliary adjective is a type of adjective that must be attached to another word for it to have any meaning.

To use らしい in this way, it must be attached to the end of a noun, and will imply that something is 'typical of (A)', where (A) is the noun that comes before it. As this らしい behaves like an い-Adjective, it may also be conjugated to らしく, before a (B) phrase will explain more about 'what' is/was typical of (A).

The primary use of this らしい is to express that (A) has some feature or trait that is expected of itself. It can be used for people, 'studying all night is so typical of Tanaka', or it can be used for things like seasons 'this heat is so typical of the Japanese Summer'. Other common translations are 'to be befitting of (A)', or 'to be appropriate for (A)'.

However, it may also be used negatively, to show that something is (often surprisingly) 'uncharacteristic of (A)'.

Fun Fact

When the noun that appears in (A) and (B) are the same, it will imply that (A) is the 'prime example of (B)', or 'the most (A), (B)'.

attributes.source: [AIAIJ] An Integrated Approach to Intermediate Japanese

Expressing hearsay or behavior using 「～らしい」

attributes.body: 的 and らしい  both describe being 'like' something, but differ in usage and nuance. 的 is highly versatile, converting nouns into な-Adjectives, e.g. 感情的な 'emotional' or 定期的に 'regularly'. In contrast, らしい  expresses embodying the ideal or typical qualities of something, e.g. 春らしい天気 'spring-like weather'.

second_relatable.title: らしい ②
second_relatable.meaning: typical of, -ish・like, appropriate for, becoming of, befitting

attributes.body: Both なりに and らしい② can connect to the idea of 'being appropriate to someone' but in different ways. なりに means “in one’s own way/to the extent of one’s ability or circumstances,” and it evaluates an action or result as the best (or at least reasonable) within those limits, as in 自分なりに考えた (‘I thought as best I could.'), and can be used in a self-deprecating sense. らしい② means 'typical' or 'true to (someone or something)', focusing on whether a behavior or style fits a person’s usual character, not on limits or 'doing one’s best', as in 彼らしくやった ('He did it how you'd expect from him.')

attributes.body: 風 and らしい② both express resemblance but differ in nuance. 風 means something has the 'air' or appearance of a type, e.g. 日本風建築 'Japanese-style architecture'. らしい② implies it embodies the ideal of that category, e.g. 日本らしい建築 implies 'quintessential Japanese architecture'.

second_relatable.title: らしい ②
second_relatable.meaning: typical of, -ish・like, appropriate for, becoming of, befitting

attributes.body: Both relate actions to what is natural or fitting, but with different nuance. らしく means 'in a way typical of' or 'true to,' judging whether behavior matches a person’s character or role, as in 彼は彼らしく行動した ('He acted in a way true to himself.'). べくして does not evaluate character but inevitability, stating that an outcome was the natural result of circumstances or causes, as in 事故は起こるべくして起こった ('The accident happened as was inevitable.').

attributes.body: Both describe attributes, but with different focuses. 型 emphasizes form or category, e.g. 家族型の会社 ('A family-style company') らしい expresses what seems typical or characteristic of something, often based on impression, e.g. 家族らしい雰囲気 ('A family-like atmosphere', warm and loving, as one might expect from a family)

attributes.body: Both describe something becoming like something else, but the nuance is different. めく・めいた means ‘showing signs of’ and refers to a noticeable change in atmosphere or appearance, without judging whether it is typical, as in 秋めいてきた ('It has started to feel autumn-like.'). らしい②, especially in らしくなってきた, focuses on becoming more typical or expected for that thing, emphasizing how well it matches the usual image, as in 秋らしくなってきた ('It has started to feel properly autumn-like.').

second_relatable.title: らしい ②
second_relatable.meaning: typical of, -ish・like, appropriate for, becoming of, befitting

attributes.body: みたいに・みたいな and らしい② both express likeness but differ in nuance. みたい suggests resemblance despite being different, e.g. 春みたいな天気 ('spring-like weather' in another season). らしい describes something that fits the typical image of what it actually is, e.g. 春らしい天気 ('weather that's just like you'd expect in spring', when it is actually spring.).

second_relatable.title: らしい ②
second_relatable.meaning: typical of, -ish・like, appropriate for, becoming of, befitting

attributes.body: らしい has two related but distinct functions. らしい ① conveys information heard from a third-party source with a nuance that the speaker believes it to be true, e.g. 雨が降るらしい ('Apparently, it's going to rain.'). らしい ② serves as an adjective, describing a typical characteristic, e.g. 春らしい天気 'spring-like weather'.

second_relatable.title: らしい ②
second_relatable.meaning: typical of, -ish・like, appropriate for, becoming of, befitting

attributes.body: っぽい and らしい② both express resemblance. っぽい is casual, like '-ish' in English, e.g. 子どもっぽい 'childish' (usually with a negative nuance). らしい② implies that someone or something embodies expected traits, e.g. 男らしい 'manly' with a nuance of fulfilling cultural expectations of what a man should be.

second_relatable.title: らしい ②
second_relatable.meaning: typical of, -ish・like, appropriate for, becoming of, befitting

attributes.body: Both relate to appearance, but with quite different nuances. ～(の)姿 refers to someone's outward form, posture, or visual state, e.g. 彼女の頑張っている姿 ('The sight/figure of her working hard'). In contrast, ～らしい② is used to describe traits or appearances typical of a category or role, e.g. 男らしい ('Manly'). While 姿 describes the appearance or form itself, ～らしい② is about how that form embodies social or cultural norms.
